feed.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion

entry.title: Combined summary - Decentralized Coinbase Payout Protocols (DCPP): A Framework for Discussion
entry.summary: Recent developments in the open-source mining ecosystem have focused on decentralized mining pool protocols such as Sv2, DATUM, and the [Open Mining Stack](https://www.256foundation.org/). These initiatives build upon previous efforts like P2Pool, which encountered significant limitations in scaling native coinbase payouts to a large and distributed miner base. A central technical challenge remains: ensuring that payout mechanisms can handle both scalability and security while navigating the constraints inherent in Bitcoin’s protocol—specifically, the limited number of coinbase outputs and scripting capabilities. Decentralized coinbase payout protocols (DCPPs) encounter three principal design obstacles. First, directly paying each miner through unique coinbase outputs is restricted by block space and output slot limits. When there are more miners than available slots, pools must determine which miners receive direct payouts, often defaulting to rewarding the largest contributors. This method introduces vulnerabilities, most notably to identity splitting attacks, where miners divide their hashrate across multiple identities to increase payout chances, thereby disadvantaging smaller participants. Such behavior leads to either unfair reward distribution or deferred settlement, placing operational and ethical strain on pool operators. Historical analysis of P2Pool reveals practical manifestations of these challenges. Data from over 2,500 blocks shows that, historically, P2Pool blocks paid between 200 and 553 addresses, constrained primarily by share difficulty and dust limits rather than explicit code-imposed rich list rules. Miners whose expected payout per block fell below a threshold saw their share difficulty increased to ensure only economically meaningful payments were included. As the pool grew, this mechanism effectively squeezed out smaller miners without any active attack against the system, demonstrating that growth alone, absent adversarial behavior, could produce outcomes similar to those caused by the Rich List Attack (RLA). Several schemes have been proposed to address these systemic issues. Chris Belcher's 2017 [payment hub model](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=2135429.0) introduced off-chain payment channels managed by a central hub, using multisig and timelocks for security. Braidpool’s [Rolling Coinbase Aggregation (RCA)](https://github.com/braidpool/braidpool/blob/8d3c5198593d691f50ae5238cdaee215f4213cda/docs/braidpool_spec.mdpayout-update) aggregates rewards into a single UTXO and periodically batches payouts with multi-party signatures. P2Poolv2 proposes a [market-driven approach](https://github.com/p2poolv2/p2poolv2/wiki/Payout-mechanism---Trading-Shares-For-Bitcoin), allowing miners to exchange sharechain UTXOs for Lightning payments via atomic swaps. Despite these innovations, vulnerabilities remain; each proposal shifts risk rather than eliminates it, exposing new vectors for payout settlement griefing (PSG) and continued susceptibility to identity splitting strategies. An ideal solution would allow every participant to claim a proportional, enforceable payout, freely transferable or swappable, with costs distributed equitably. However, Bitcoin's current scripting and covenant limitations make such a fully trustless system unfeasible. Practical designs must therefore strike a balance between fairness, technical feasibility, and protection against strategic manipulation. Two fundamental tools—Bitcoin script and external hashrate or liquidity markets—form the basis of contemporary approaches. For example, a coinpool funded directly from the coinbase could rely on pre-signed exit transactions, but careful governance of pooled keys and robust fallback mechanisms are required to prevent malicious control or gridlock. Case studies applying existing coinpool structures within the P2Poolv2 framework, such as Spark and Ark, illustrate both opportunities and risks. In models where a set of service providers and market makers collectively manage payout outputs, the system becomes vulnerable to attackers inflating their presence through multiple identities—a “poison pill” attack—forcing honest actors to assume additional liabilities. In considering how to structure fair value-weighted draws, it is critical that the probability of selection for payout slots is strictly proportional to the actual claim size, regardless of how claims are divided among identities. Otherwise, large miners retain an advantage by splitting claims, perpetuating the RLA as a probabilistic game and marginalizing smaller miners. Additionally, the source of randomness used to allocate payouts must be resistant to manipulation; seeds derived from prior Bitcoin blocks are preferable to those from the sharechain, as they are harder to bias through cheap grinding. The persistence of these design challenges underscores the complexity of developing scalable, equitable, and secure decentralized payout systems for mining pools. The evolution of these architectures continues, shaped by lessons from historical implementations and ongoing research into cryptographic protocols, incentive alignment, and governance. Extensive resources, including glossary explanations for terms like DCPP, PSG, and RLA, are available at [learnbitcoin.com](https://www.learnbitcoin.com/glossary/decentralized%20coinbase%20payout%20
